The Story of Concealment

I bow to Lord Jina, the omniscient, in whose supreme knowledge the entire world appears like an atom, and I write a story about concealment — about not stating things as they are, about hiding the truth.

King Dhritisheen of Ujjain and Queen Malayavati had a son named Chandpradyot. He was as handsome as he was virtuous. Through the ripening of merit, he possessed all means of happiness. Once, a learned Brahmin named Kalsandiv from the city of Benatatt in the southern land came to Ujjain. He knew several languages. Therefore, Dhritisheen kept him to teach Chandpradyot.

After teaching the prince several languages, Kalsandiv began teaching him a mlechchha (barbarian) language. The pronunciation of this language was very difficult. The prince had great difficulty learning it. One day, a lesson came with very difficult pronunciation. The prince could not pronounce it correctly. Kalsandiv tried hard to teach him the correct pronunciation but did not succeed. This made Kalsandiv somewhat angry. In his anger, he kicked the prince.

Chandpradyot was, after all, a prince, and his temper also flared. He said to his teacher, "Very well, sir, you have kicked me. I too will not rest until I take revenge for this. Let me become king, and then you will see — I will cut off this very foot of yours!" Truly, children are short-sighted.

Kalsandiv stayed some more days and then went south. Later, Kalsandiv had the opportunity to hear a monk's discourse. Hearing it, he became deeply detached. He became a monk.

Meanwhile, King Dhritisheen too handed all state affairs to Chandpradyot and became a monk. The reins of government came into Chandpradyot's hands. There is no doubt that Chandpradyot governed with great wisdom. He left nothing undone for the welfare of his subjects.

One day, a letter came to Chandpradyot from a Yavan (Greek) king. The language was barbarian. No royal official could read it. Then the king saw it and he could read it. Reading the letter, the king felt great devotion for his teacher Kalsandiv. He realised that it was because of Kalsandiv that he could understand this difficult language.

The king immediately sent messengers to find Kalsandiv. They found him practising austerities in a forest. The king went personally, bowed to his teacher, and said, "Gurudev, in my childhood, in anger, I threatened to cut off your foot. Now that I am king, I must fulfil my word." Kalsandiv smiled and said, "My child, I have already renounced this body through monastic life. This foot is no longer mine to keep or lose. But your sincerity in keeping your word, even after so many years, shows your noble character."

The king then asked his teacher's forgiveness for his childhood threat. Kalsandiv blessed him and continued on his spiritual path. Both teacher and student, through their respective paths, ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the words spoken in childhood anger should be acknowledged and addressed. King Chandpradyot, despite his great power, honoured his childhood threat by seeking out his teacher. But the teacher, having transcended worldly attachments through monastic life, showed that true forgiveness and understanding go beyond such worldly concerns. The wise should practise honesty and not conceal their true intentions.
